newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Guatemalans win EU aid to support peace plan.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalans win EU aid to support peace plan.

text.p: The European Union on Tuesday pledged over $250 million to Guatemala to help the Central American nation rebuild after three decades of civil war.

"This (aid package) will help strengthen the European Union's role as a player and partner in the peace process," said Manuel Marin, European Commissioner responsible for relations with Latin America.

Marin was speaking at a news conference with Guatemalan President Alvaro Arzu who is in Europe to promote plans to implement an ambitious peace treaty signed on December 29 between the government and leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) rebels.

The Guatemalan government has calculated it needs some $2.5 billion for programmes to modernise the state, combat poverty and resettle hundreds of thousands of Guatemalans displaced during 36 years of conflict.
On Tuesday Marin pledged $250 million in grants and the Inter-American Development Bank's special European Office announced it would supplement this with two loans totalling $50 million.
Arzu told the news conference he was grateful for the assistance, but warned: "The mere signing of the peace agreement will not bring everything from heaven.
"We shall encounter difficulties ... as we have on the long road that brought us here," he said.

Marin said details of how the EU would like to see its grants spent would only be finalised in the next few days, but Arzu said Guatemala had already identified key priorities for rebuilding the country.
"We need to lower our internal debt, this is clear," he said. "Infrastructure and development are also areas we would like to direct aid towards."

At the same news conference Guatemala denied it had struck a deal with China to break off diplomatic relations with Taiwan in exchange for Beijing not vetoing a United Nations mission to the Central American country.
"Absolutely and categorically Guatemala maintains full diplomatic relations with Taiwan," said Foreign Minister Eduardo Stein. "This has never been the subject of negotiations with China."
Stein was speaking a day after the U.N. Security Council unanimously approved sending 155 military observers to Guatemala to monitor the peace accords.
China had vetoed an earlier vote because of Guatemala's strong links to Taiwan, but relented after 10 days of intense negotiations.

In a statement, the Inter-American Development Bank said it would grant Guatemala two loans -- one for $17 million over 30 years at variable interest with a four-year grace period and the other for $33 million in local currency for 40 years with interest at one percent for 10 years and two percent thereafter.
The EU's $250 million grant covers 1997-2000 with some $50 million made available each year.
Under the peace agreements, the Guatemalan army is to cut its numbers and about 3,000 guerrillas from the URNG are to go to assembly points, disarm and be integrated into civilian life.
